Maybe you are a principled soul who believes in sportsmanship, so you never cheat at video games. For the rest of us, I want to talk about the games that motivate you to cheat - regardless of whether or not you end up cheating.

Most of us have heard of "flow" from a Hungarian called "Chicks send me high" or something like that:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihaly_Csikszentmihalyi

The idea of "flow" suggests that a game must not be too easy or too hard, or else it won't be fun. A few lucky people never feel bored when they feel frustrated; for most of us, frustration also induces boredom, so whenever a game frustrates us, it also bores us. Unfortunately, games are usually designed in distract us and pull us into habit-forming Skinner boxes, so a lot of games will destroy your time (and mental health) with boredom but keep you engaged enough to continue throwing good time after bad.

Some video game cheat systems arise because hardcore AAA gamers have developed gaming skills, and AAA studios often develop games that can only be played by people with highly developed skills appropriate to existing games. The few truly skilled gamers can cruise through the entire game and complain that they are not challenged enough, whereas unskillful players resort to save-scumming, trainer programs, internal cheat codes, and the like. The highly skilled gamers sometimes express hatred for cheaters - but then again, many gamers express a lot of hatred for a lot of things, so maybe hatred for game cheaters doesn't mean much in context.

With some games, I feel that the challenge and the incentives are perfectly balanced. With those games, I am perfectly engaged and I never think about cheating, but those are few and far between. With other games, the incentives draw me in, but my skills are not adequate to play the game as it was designed, so I can either cheat or quit. (Dishonored and Dishonored 2 come to mind: the visually lush whalepunk atmosphere draws me in, but I don't have the skills to play the games properly. Lush visual design does not motivate me to develop stealth skills.)

However, most commonly, the problem that incentivizes me to cheat is not difficulty. The most common problem is padding. A hell of a lot of AAA games include boring gameplay, often stretched out with poorly-skippable cutscenes. I have sufficient skills to beat these games, but it feels like a chore. In such games, cheat codes can allow a quick overview of any interesting parts of the game, and sometimes the visuals or the story are compelling enough to make the cheating worthwhile. However, cheating through a boring game to get to an interesting story is not a "flow" experience - it's basically reading a book that requires a cheat code to turn each page.

When a game is basically a melodramatic story with eye-catching visual art and boring gameplay, I don't mind the flow-killing effort of cheating. A few games try to be "short and sweet," and even though they start to bore me before they are done, they are short enough that I still enjoy playing them to the end. (Vigilantes by TimeSlip comes to mind. It's a short, minimalist game; the thrill wears off a few hours before the end, but it delivers a lot of fun up front and it doesn't wear out its welcome.) A common experience, however, is that a AAA game will draw me in with an interesting premise, and then bore me to tears until I am willing to cheat. If am willing to cheat at a bad game out of mere curiosity, I am better off watching a youtube video to spoil the surprises of gameplay.

For many people, what is intrinsically fun shifts around from day to day. On Tuesday I might feel a need for an eight-hour session of SimCity, but by Thursday I might demand Bioshock. The best course of action (in my arrogant opinion) is to keep watch on your own boredom and don't commit too many hours to any game out of habit. Don't throw good time after bad. If a game doesn't give you intrinsically fun gameplay in the first few hours, ask yourself whether you could get more intrinsic fun out of some other game. If a game doesn't seem intrinsically fun today, it might seem intrinsically fun next week.
The test of intrinsic fun is whether you ever feel inclined to cheat past the challenge

Cheating in single player games, huh? I haven't thought about it much, but through my past, I can only really remember cheats in GTA/other open world games.

If you need to cheat in single player games in order to progress, you should probably just stop playing that game and watch a video on it instead, since you are robbing yourself of the experience that the devs tried to lay out. Dark Souls/likes, open world, platforming, they (should) have been designed without cheats in mind. If you want to play what you paid for, you should try to play without cheats.

Obviously if you're just using random cheats for fun or because it's funny, then that doesn't apply until you start doing it in multiplayer games.

Back in the days, when I first played Doom and Doom II, I sucked at them. I liked what I saw, but going around shooting demons from hell while solving puzzles was too much for me. So I enabled godmode and the occasional noclipping to explore the levels at my own pace, just enjoying that part of the game without being bothered by the enemies. I beat the entire game that way and had fun. (Not all secrets, though.) After that, I did the whole game on the easiest setting without cheats and beat it again - while having fun. It was the same game, but this time with enemies that can kill you! And then I beat it again on the next difficulty setting and the next one, until I was just totally annihilated on the nightmare difficulty. I never beat Doom II on the highest difficulty.

For those who do not know, every enemy respawns after like a minute. Doesn't matter if you killed him or not. A few minutes in and the whole map is just covered with monsters. The only way to beat Doom on the highest difficult setting is through speedrunning (afaik) while avoiding enemies. But I hate rushing, so I never bothered doing that. I like taking my time and exploring, so having godmode the first time around was awesome and I still play it like that from time to time. I probably beat Doom II over 50 times.

Good games allow you to have fun in more way than just "the standard way to play through the game". The absolute best games don't only allow stuff like sequence breaking, but specifically build things in a way to enable it after you are skilled enough. Like the wall jumps or infinite morph ball jumps in Metroid III. That's how you keep having fun after having beat the game dozen of times already. That and setting up additional rules, like beating Wolfenstein 3D only with the knife, only to break that rule on the first boss, because you realize it would take like half an hour to take him out that way and that's boring as fuck.
